summary:
ORBIT: The Last Little Outpost is a free browser game built for the challenge "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer": it trains children aged 7–12 to think like an astronaut. Players command a lunar South Pole outpost for five days, directing two crew members and keeping four resources alive: power, oxygen, water and food.

Each room teaches one real concept through a short puzzle: splitting water into oxygen, recycling water, aiming solar panels, growing plants, and shielding a shelter from solar storms. After every fix, a NASA fact about that same system appears with a picture, and a different one shows on each replay. Storms are built from NASA's DONKI space-weather records, some facts come from NASA OSDR studies, and every NASA-derived item is labelled live, cached, archived or simulated, so children learn what is data and what is game.

The key skill is prioritisation. When a power fault leaves only four reserve bolts, players must choose what to save first as the clock runs down.

It matters because learning by doing builds curiosity, planning under pressure and systems thinking. Game rules, such as storm timing, are disclosed as simplifications.
details:
ORBIT: The Last Little Outpost is a real-time browser game for children aged 7–12. Players command a lunar South Pole outpost for five 90-second days, directing two crew members, Bolt and Luna, and keeping four resources alive: power, oxygen, water and food. Each room has one puzzle based on real science: an oxygen maker that splits water into oxygen and hydrogen, water-recycling pipes, aiming a solar panel at the Sun, growing food in real time, and choosing materials to shield a radiation shelter. Scheduled red alerts (power cable faults, leaks, solar storms) force quick decisions. After every fix, a NASA fact about that same machine appears with a picture, and a different fact shows each time.

NASA data. Solar storms are built from NASA DONKI space-weather records, fetched live. Plant facts and discovery cards use NASA OSDR studies, Moon science uses Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter findings, and photographs come from the NASA Image and Video Library. Every NASA-derived item is labelled live, cached, archived or simulated, and the game falls back to archived real records if NASA is unreachable.

Benefits and impact. Children practise prioritising scarce resources under pressure, delegating to a crew, and connecting everyday science to life in space. New facts on every replay prompt curiosity. It is free, needs no account, and collects no data.

Creativity. It takes the quick-task, red-alert rhythm of popular crew games and makes every task a real piece of astronaut life. Consequences teach: a cable fault leaves four reserve bolts to share, zero oxygen starts a 40-second countdown, and crew can be lost in a storm.

Tools. TypeScript, React, Phaser 3, Vite, Zustand and the Web Audio API; tested with Vitest and Playwright; deployed with GitHub Actions and Pages. Built with SI assistance (Claude, Anthropic).

Factors considered. Honesty: game rules are disclosed (storm harm in five seconds is a simplification; DONKI does not measure Moon radiation dose). Accessibility: status shown by shape and word, not colour alone; keyboard and touch play; reduced-motion and larger-text options. Resilience: works when NASA services are down. Reading load: pictures and short captions. Next step: testing with children, which has not happened yet.
